procedures.title: Awake Fiberoptic Intubation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: The controlled, spontaneously-breathing approach to the anticipated difficult airway — topicalize, sedate lightly, scope while the patient protects their own airway.
procedures.description: Controlled airway access preserving spontaneous ventilation.

blocks.html:
• Anticipated difficult airway (limited mouth opening, cervical spine immobility, airway mass/distortion, prior difficult intubation history)
  • Need to preserve spontaneous ventilation through the intubation process
  • Unstable cervical spine where direct laryngoscopy positioning is contraindicated
  • Upper airway pathology (tumor, abscess, angioedema) where induction could precipitate total obstruction

• Uncooperative patient unable to tolerate awake instrumentation (relative — may require heavier sedation or an alternative plan)
  • Actively vomiting or high aspiration risk with an unprotected, un-topicalized airway
  • Rapidly deteriorating airway where the time cost of awake technique is not survivable — move to a faster rescue plan (surgical airway) instead
  • Known severe local anesthetic allergy limiting topicalization options (relative — alternative agents exist)

• Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope with light source and monitor
  • Topical local anesthetic (nebulized and/or direct application: lidocaine 2-4%)
  • Atomizer or nebulizer device for topicalization
  • Antisialagogue (glycopyrrolate) given in advance to dry secretions and improve visualization
  • Light or titrated sedation agents (dexmedetomidine, low-dose midazolam/fentanyl) preserving spontaneous respiration
  • Appropriately sized ETT preloaded on the scope
  • Full difficult airway cart on standby

steps.html: Administer antisialagogue early enough to dry secretions before topicalization begins.

Topicalize the airway systematically: nares (if nasal approach), oropharynx, and progressively deeper structures using nebulized and direct local anesthetic application, often via a “spray as you go” technique through the scope's working channel.
Titrate light sedation to maintain a cooperative, spontaneously breathing patient — the goal is comfort and cooperation, not unconsciousness.
Preload the ETT onto the bronchoscope shaft.
Advance the scope through the chosen route (oral or nasal), maintaining midline orientation and continuously advancing toward the glottis under direct vision.
Identify the vocal cords and advance the scope tip through the glottis into the trachea, confirming tracheal rings and carina view.
Railroad the ETT over the scope into the trachea.
Confirm depth and position, withdraw the scope, confirm placement (EtCO2, bilateral breath sounds), secure the tube.
Only proceed to induction of general anesthesia once tracheal placement is confirmed — this is the entire safety rationale for the awake technique.

blocks.title: Sedation depth is the whole safety margin
blocks.html: The entire value of this technique is that the patient keeps breathing for themselves throughout — titrate sedation conservatively, since oversedation converts a controlled awake technique into an unplanned loss of airway.

• Inadequate topicalization causing patient discomfort, coughing, or laryngospasm during the procedure
  • Oversedation converting a spontaneously breathing awake technique into an unplanned loss of airway
  • Secretions or bleeding obscuring the fiberoptic view — antisialagogue and gentle technique mitigate this
  • Prolonged procedure time in a patient who cannot tolerate delay — recognize early when to abandon for a faster rescue plan
  • Esophageal misidentification if orientation is lost — maintain constant visual confirmation of airway structures

The entire value of this technique is that the patient keeps breathing for themselves throughout — protect that at all costs by titrating sedation conservatively.

“Spray as you go” topicalization through the working channel keeps you from having to stop and re-dose separately — it's more efficient and better tolerated.

Have a clear abort criterion decided before you start: if topicalization or scope advancement isn't progressing within a reasonable window, move to the backup plan rather than persisting.

This is a skill that degrades fast without practice — simulation reps on a mannequin keep the scope-handling reflexes sharp between real cases.

procedures.title: Cricothyrotomy — Surgical, Percutaneous & Needle
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: Three techniques for one problem: Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate. Adapted from the author's original “Introduction to Surgical Airways” teaching deck, used with permission.
procedures.description: Surgical, percutaneous, and needle techniques for CICO.

blocks.html:
• Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate (CICO)
  • Artificial airway obstruction (device failure, blocked ETT/trach)
  • Pathologic airway obstruction (angioedema, trauma, burns, abnormal anatomy) not amenable to oral/nasal intubation
  • Failure of primary and rescue airway techniques when oxygenation cannot otherwise be achieved

• A viable, faster alternative airway exists (relative — in true CICO there are no absolute contraindications to a front-of-neck airway)
  • Pediatric patients under ~1 year for needle/surgical cricothyrotomy — anatomy strongly favors alternative approaches where any other option exists
  • Distorted or unidentifiable anterior neck anatomy (relative — may require the scalpel-finger-bougie approach over needle-based techniques)

Needle cricothyrotomy

  • Large-bore needle/angiocath (12–14 ga)
  • 3 mm ID ETT connector/BVM adaptor
  • 3-way stopcock, jet insufflation source

Percutaneous (Seldinger) cricothyrotomy

  • Introducer needle, flexible guidewire, dilator
  • Cricothyrotomy tube or ETT

Surgical (open) cricothyrotomy

  • #10 scalpel, bougie
  • Cuffed ETT or cricothyrotomy tube
Needle cricothyrotomy

steps.html: Palpate and stabilize the cricothyroid membrane.
Insert large-bore needle/angiocath through the membrane at a caudad angle, aspirating for air to confirm tracheal placement.
Advance catheter, remove needle, secure.
Connect 3 mm ID ETT adaptor and 3-way stopcock to an oxygen/jet insufflation source.
Ventilate via jet insufflation — expect a prolonged expiratory phase due to narrow-lumen exhalation limitation.
Treat as a temporizing measure only — plan definitive airway within ~45 minutes to avoid progressive hypercarbia; this is the primary technique of choice in pediatric patients due to small anatomy.

blocks.html: Percutaneous (Seldinger) cricothyrotomy

steps.html: Palpate and stabilize the cricothyroid membrane.
Insert introducer needle through the membrane, confirm tracheal entry (air aspiration).
Thread flexible guidewire through the needle into the trachea; remove needle, leaving wire in place.
Make a small vertical skin incision superficial to the membrane.
Advance dilator over the guidewire to expand the tract through the membrane.
Remove dilator; advance cricothyrotomy tube or ETT over the wire into the trachea.
Remove wire, confirm placement, secure tube.
Slower than the surgical technique — not the preferred choice when seconds matter most in a true CICO emergency.

blocks.html: Surgical (open) cricothyrotomy

steps.html: Palpate and stabilize the cricothyroid membrane with non-dominant hand, maintaining laryngeal control throughout.
Make a vertical skin incision superficial to the membrane.
Insert the scalpel laterally through the cricothyroid membrane itself, then rotate/withdraw to open the tract.
Insert a finger along the blunt side of the scalpel to maintain the opening and confirm tracheal entry by feel.
Insert a bougie alongside the finger into the trachea.
Railroad a cuffed ETT or cricothyrotomy tube over the bougie into the trachea.
Remove bougie, inflate cuff, confirm placement (chest rise, EtCO2, auscultation), secure tube.

blocks.title: Declare it, then commit
blocks.html: The biggest driver of a bad CICO outcome is hesitation to escalate, not technique failure — once the front-of-neck decision is made, further attempts at oral intubation or mask ventilation only cost the time the procedure needs.

• Delayed recognition of CICO — the biggest driver of bad outcomes is hesitation to escalate, not technique failure
  • Needle cricothyrotomy: hypercarbia beyond the ~45-minute usable window due to inadequate exhalation through a narrow lumen
  • False passage (paratracheal placement) — confirm with air aspiration/tactile feel before committing to dilation or tube passage
  • Percutaneous technique speed — the Seldinger sequence costs time that may not exist in true CICO; know when to default to open technique
  • Pediatric anatomy makes the open surgical technique disproportionately difficult for inexperienced providers — needle technique is the default in this population
  • Bleeding obscuring the field, especially with vascular anterior neck anatomy

If you're doing a front-of-neck airway, you've already failed two other airway plans — commit fully and move fast, don't second-guess the decision mid-procedure.

The finger-bougie technique in open cricothyrotomy is what actually confirms you're in the trachea — trust tactile feel over visual confirmation in a bloody or dark field.

Needle technique buys time in kids and true emergencies; it is not a destination airway. Know your institution's definitive airway plan before you start.

Practice the open technique on a model regularly — this is a low-frequency, high-stakes skill where muscle memory under stress is the entire game.

procedures.title: Front-of-Neck Rescue Airway in CICO
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: The decision framework that sits above the individual techniques — recognizing CICO fast, and choosing the right front-of-neck approach without hesitation.
procedures.description: The decision framework above the individual techniques.

blocks.html:
• Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate (CICO) confirmed after failed attempts at face mask ventilation, supraglottic airway placement, and tracheal intubation
  • Progressive desaturation despite optimized attempts at the above
  • Any scenario where the algorithm has been exhausted and oxygenation cannot be achieved by any other route

• None — by definition, if the diagnosis of CICO is correct, a front-of-neck airway is indicated; the only real contraindication is misdiagnosing the situation as CICO when another maneuver would still work

• Pre-designated CICO/difficult airway cart, immediately available and known to the team
  • Scalpel-bougie-tube setup as the primary adult technique (see Cricothyrotomy entry)
  • Needle cricothyrotomy/jet ventilation setup for pediatric or anatomy-limited cases
  • Clear cognitive aid posted or immediately accessible (CICO algorithm card)

steps.html: Declare CICO out loud to the team the moment it is recognized — verbalizing the diagnosis is what triggers the algorithm shift and mobilizes help.
Call for the difficult airway/CICO cart immediately if not already open.

Default to the scalpel-bougie-tube (surgical cricothyrotomy) technique in adults as the fastest, most reliable front-of-neck approach — do not default to needle techniques or percutaneous kits when speed is the priority.
In pediatric patients or anatomy where surgical technique is disproportionately difficult, default to needle cricothyrotomy with jet ventilation instead.
Execute the chosen technique without further attempts at oral intubation or mask ventilation — going back to a failed technique wastes the only resource that matters, time.
Confirm oxygenation via the front-of-neck airway before considering the emergency resolved.
Debrief and plan definitive airway management (OR-based conversion, tracheostomy) once the patient is stabilized.

blocks.title: The hard part is the decision, not the scalpel
blocks.html: Rehearse saying "this is CICO, we are moving to a surgical airway" out loud in simulation — a pre-briefed team with a known default technique moves faster than the smartest individual improvising alone.

• Delayed declaration of CICO — teams often persist with failing techniques past the point they should have escalated
  • Choosing a slower technique (percutaneous/Seldinger) when the situation calls for the fastest option (surgical)
  • Fixation on a single failed approach instead of moving decisively to the front-of-neck algorithm
  • Team communication breakdown — if CICO isn't declared out loud, help doesn't mobilize in time

The hardest part of CICO management isn't the scalpel technique — it's the decision to commit to it. Practice saying “this is CICO, we are moving to a surgical airway” out loud in simulation so it isn't the first time in a real event.

This entry is the decision layer sitting above the individual techniques (see Cricothyrotomy) — know both, but know this framework first.

A pre-briefed team with a known cart location and a known default technique moves faster than the smartest individual improvising alone.

procedures.title: Percutaneous / Surgical Tracheostomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: The definitive-airway conversation, not the crisis-moment tool. Adapted from the author's original “Introduction to Surgical Airways” teaching deck, used with permission.
procedures.description: Definitive long-term airway, not a rescue technique.

blocks.html:
• Long-term ventilator-assisted respiration anticipated
  • Failure to wean or prolonged weaning from mechanical ventilation
  • Inability to protect the airway with an anticipated prolonged course
  • Definitive airway control following cricothyrotomy as a bridge (conversion to tracheostomy once stabilized)

• Emergent CICO scenario — tracheostomy is not the front-line rescue airway; cricothyrotomy is faster and anatomically more accessible in a crisis
  • Uncorrected coagulopathy for elective/semi-elective percutaneous approach (relative)
  • Distorted neck anatomy or inability to access the site (favors surgical/open approach in a controlled setting, e.g., OR)

• Scalpel, retractors, dissection instruments, suction, tracheostomy tube, suture
  • OR setting typically required — this is a controlled, planned procedure, not a rapid rescue technique
  • Bronchoscopic guidance where available for the percutaneous dilational approach
Open surgical tracheostomy

steps.html: Position patient supine with neck extended (if not contraindicated by cervical spine precautions).
Identify the site — closer to the sternoclavicular notch than the cricothyroid membrane, at approximately the 2nd–3rd tracheal ring level.
Make a transverse or vertical skin incision as per surgeon preference/institutional protocol.
Perform meticulous dissection through the strap muscles, retracting to expose the thyroid isthmus.
Divide or retract the thyroid isthmus as needed to expose the trachea.
Hold the field open with retractors.
Create the tracheal opening at the bottom of the 3rd and top of the 4th tracheal ring — excise a small window rather than a complete tracheal ring resection.
Insert the tracheostomy tube into the created opening.
Confirm placement (chest rise, EtCO2, bilateral breath sounds).
Secure the tube, dress the site.

blocks.title: This is not a rescue airway
blocks.html: Tracheostomy belongs to the planned, definitive-airway conversation once a patient is stabilized — attempting it as a first response in a true CICO emergency costs time that cricothyrotomy does not.

• Not a rapid rescue airway — attempting tracheostomy in a true CICO emergency costs time that cricothyrotomy does not
  • Requires an OR in the standard surgical approach — logistically incompatible with emergent bedside crisis management outside specific percutaneous bedside protocols
  • More destructive/invasive than cricothyrotomy — greater tissue disruption, longer procedure time, higher bleeding risk from the thyroid isthmus and surrounding vasculature
  • Over-resection of tracheal rings — removing a fully transected ring segment is a technical error; the opening should be a window, not a full ring excision
  • Bleeding from thyroid isthmus if not adequately controlled during dissection/division

If the question is “can this patient breathe right now,” the answer is cricothyrotomy, not tracheostomy — tracheostomy belongs to the planned, definitive-airway conversation.

Site selection matters: too high risks subglottic stenosis and interferes with a prior cricothyrotomy site; too low risks innominate vessel injury.

When converting a crisis cricothyrotomy to a definitive tracheostomy, this is typically done electively in a controlled OR setting once the patient is stabilized.

procedures.title: Retrograde Intubation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: A backup technique for the difficult airway when fiberoptic and video laryngoscopy aren't available or aren't working — a wire from below guiding the tube from above.
procedures.description: Wire-guided backup when fiberoptic/video fails.

blocks.html:
• Difficult airway where standard laryngoscopy and video-assisted techniques have failed or are unavailable
  • Significant blood or secretions obscuring the glottic view for fiberoptic technique
  • Limited mouth opening where a rigid scope cannot be introduced but the cricothyroid membrane is accessible
  • Resource-limited settings without fiberoptic or video laryngoscopy equipment

• True CICO emergency — this technique is too slow; go directly to a surgical airway
  • Coagulopathy or overlying infection at the cricothyroid membrane puncture site (relative)
  • Distorted or unidentifiable anterior neck anatomy preventing safe membrane puncture
  • Any faster airway option is available and appropriate — retrograde intubation is a backup, not a first-line technique

• Introducer needle (similar to percutaneous cricothyrotomy kit)
  • Long guidewire or epidural catheter
  • Retrieval forceps or hemostat
  • Standard ETT
  • Local anesthetic if patient is awake/cooperative

steps.html: Identify and stabilize the cricothyroid membrane.
Puncture the membrane with the introducer needle, directed cephalad, confirming tracheal entry by air aspiration.
Thread the guidewire or epidural catheter through the needle, advancing it cephalad through the larynx and into the oropharynx.
Retrieve the wire from the mouth (or nose, depending on technique) using direct visualization, laryngoscopy, or forceps.
Thread the ETT over the retrieved wire in an antegrade fashion, advancing it down toward the larynx.
Advance the ETT into the trachea while withdrawing/releasing the wire at the neck puncture site as the tube passes the cords.
Once the tube is through the cords and into the trachea, remove the wire entirely.
Confirm placement (EtCO2, chest rise, auscultation), secure the tube, manage the neck puncture site.

blocks.title: Know where this sits on the urgency ladder
blocks.html: This technique is slower than fiberoptic or video laryngoscopy and far slower than a surgical airway — in a true CICO emergency, skip straight to cricothyrotomy rather than starting here.

• Technique is time-consuming relative to other rescue options — poor choice when seconds matter most
  • Wire retrieval failure or loss of wire position during tube advancement
  • Bleeding at the puncture site obscuring the field
  • Tube may catch at the glottic inlet advancing over the wire — gentle rotation and steady wire tension help guide it through
  • False sense of security delaying escalation to a surgical airway if the technique is struggling

This sits between fiberoptic technique and a surgical airway on the urgency spectrum — know your algorithm's place for it before you need it.

A firecracker-fast true CICO scenario should skip straight to cricothyrotomy; retrograde intubation belongs to the difficult-but-not-yet-critical airway.

Have a clear mental time limit for this technique — if it isn't progressing, abandon it for a surgical airway rather than persisting past the point of safety.

procedures.title: Chest Tube Placement (Tube Thoracostomy)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: A full open technique for hemothorax and pneumothorax — from site selection through the post-placement film and removal timing.
procedures.description: Full open technique for hemo/pneumothorax.

blocks.html:
• Pneumothorax (simple, traumatic, or post-finger-thoracostomy definitive management)
  • Hemothorax
  • Traumatic hemopneumothorax
  • Empyema or complicated pleural effusion requiring drainage (non-emergent variant of the same technique)

• No absolute contraindications in a true emergent pneumothorax/hemothorax with hemodynamic compromise
  • Relative: coagulopathy (correct if time permits and patient is stable enough), diaphragmatic hernia at the intended site (imaging guidance preferred if not emergent), extensive pleural adhesions (may require alternate site or surgical approach)

• 2% chlorhexidine solution, sterile gauze, sterile drapes
  • Local anesthetic (if patient status allows)
  • Chest tube, 32–36 Fr for adult trauma/hemothorax indications
  • Two clamps/forceps, #10 scalpel
  • Kelly clamp (or equivalent) for blunt dissection
  • Suture for securing the tube
  • Pleural drainage system (e.g., Pleurovac)
  • Petroleum-based gauze, additional sterile gauze, pressure dressing supplies

steps.html: Position the patient supine or semi-recumbent with the arm raised over the head to expose the lateral chest wall.
Identify the insertion site — typically the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line, at or above the level of the nipple.
Consider local anesthetic depending on patient status.
Sterilize widely with 2% chlorhexidine; create a large sterile field with sterile gauze; drape, exposing only the marked area.
Grasp the proximal free end of the chest tube (32–36 Fr) with a clamp/forceps and the distal tip with another — do not let instrument tips pass the end of the tube.
Make a 1.5–3.0 cm incision with a #10 scalpel, parallel to the rib, through subcutaneous tissue to the level of the intercostal muscles.
Bluntly dissect superiorly with a Kelly clamp, tunneling up to the intercostal space directly above the rib — stay off the inferior rib margin to avoid the subcostal neurovascular bundle.
At the intercostal space, position the clamp tips at the superior rib edge and apply firm, controlled pressure to pass through the parietal pleura (this may require significant force).
Insert a finger into the thoracic space to confirm thoracostomy and check for adhesions or unanticipated findings.
Insert the chest tube along the dissected tract, directing it apically/posteriorly for fluid or anteriorly/superiorly for pneumothorax evacuation.
Advance until the last side hole is within the pleural space, with the proximal hole at least 2 cm beyond the rib margin — skin-level marker typically 10–14 cm in an average adult.
Secure with mattress or interrupted sutures on both sides of the incision, snugging tissue around the tube for an air-tight seal; wrap suture around the tube twice and tie.
Connect to a sterile pleural drainage system at initial suction of –20 cm H2O; unclamp the distal end once connected.
Tape the tube to the patient's side; dress with petroleum-based gauze, additional sterile gauze, and pressure dressings.
Obtain an AP chest radiograph to confirm placement and monitor for complications (bleeding, hemothorax, air leak, organ perforation).
Time removal based on the original indication; obtain a follow-up chest radiograph 12–24 hours after removal.

blocks.title: The finger check before tube passage is non-negotiable
blocks.html: It's the difference between confirmed pleural entry and a blind pass into an unexpected structure — skipping it to save seconds is the step most likely to cause an organ injury.

• Neurovascular bundle injury from dissecting along the inferior rib margin instead of the superior edge
  • Organ perforation (lung, liver, spleen, diaphragm) from excessive force or poor trajectory control
  • Malposition — tube kinking, insufficient insertion depth, or a side hole left outside the pleural space
  • Inadequate seal at the skin leading to air leak or subcutaneous emphysema
  • Infection from break in sterile technique, particularly relevant in non-emergent placements
  • Failure to confirm with a finger sweep before tube passage — this is the step that catches adhesions and confirms true pleural entry

The finger check before tube insertion is non-negotiable — it's the difference between confirmed pleural entry and a blind pass into an unexpected structure.

Direction after entry matters clinically: apical/posterior for air, basilar/posterior for fluid — but in an emergent trauma placement, adequate drainage of the acute threat takes priority over perfect directional placement.

Firm, controlled pressure through the pleura is expected — hesitation here often causes more tissue trauma than a confident, controlled pass.

Don't skip the post-placement film — it's the only way to confirm true intrathoracic position and catch a missed complication before it becomes clinically significant.

procedures.title: Finger Thoracostomy / Needle Decompression
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: Immediate decompression of tension pneumothorax — the bridge to a formal chest tube, not a replacement for one.
procedures.description: Immediate tension pneumothorax decompression.

blocks.html:
• Clinically diagnosed tension pneumothorax: hypotension, absent/decreased breath sounds unilaterally, tracheal deviation (late finding), distended neck veins, respiratory distress in a trauma or critically ill patient
  • Diagnosis is clinical — do not delay for imaging in a decompensating patient with a compatible presentation

• None absolute in a true tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic compromise — the risk of inaction outweighs procedural risk
  • Misdiagnosis (simple pneumothorax without tension physiology) is the real risk to guard against, not a formal contraindication

Needle decompression

  • Large-bore needle/angiocath (10-14 ga, adequate length for chest wall thickness — standard needles are frequently too short in larger patients)

Finger thoracostomy

  • Scalpel, Kelly clamp or equivalent for blunt dissection
  • Gloves, basic sterile prep if time allows (do not delay for this in a decompensating patient)
Needle decompression

steps.html: Identify the insertion site — traditionally 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, though 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line (same site as finger thoracostomy) is increasingly preferred given shorter chest wall distance and lower vascular injury risk.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the chest wall, just above the rib margin, advancing until a rush of air or loss of resistance is felt.
Listen/feel for the hallmark rush of air confirming tension physiology and successful decompression.
Secure the catheter in place; this is a temporizing measure — a formal chest tube (tube thoracostomy) is required promptly after.

blocks.html: Finger thoracostomy

steps.html: Identify the same site as tube thoracostomy — 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line.
Make an incision through skin and subcutaneous tissue with a scalpel.
Bluntly dissect with a Kelly clamp to the pleura, staying superior to the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
Puncture through the pleura with the clamp or a finger, feeling for the rush of air.
Sweep a finger into the pleural space to confirm decompression and clear any adhesions.
Leave the tract open or pack loosely until a formal chest tube can be placed — this technique can serve as decompression alone or as the first step of a full tube thoracostomy.

blocks.title: This is a clinical diagnosis and a clinical decompression
blocks.html: Don't wait for a chest X-ray in a patient who is actively decompensating — a needle that's too short to reach the pleural space is a common, preventable cause of a failed decompression in larger patients.

• Needle too short to reach the pleural space in patients with a thick chest wall — a common cause of failed decompression
  • Vascular or lung injury from an overly medial or poorly angled needle insertion
  • False negative (no rush of air) does not rule out tension pneumothorax — reassess clinically and consider finger thoracostomy or repeat attempt at an alternate site
  • Needle decompression alone is temporizing only — failure to follow with a formal chest tube risks recurrence

Finger thoracostomy at the 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line site is increasingly favored over the classic 2nd intercostal space needle site — shorter distance to the pleura, more reliable decompression in larger patients.

This is a clinical diagnosis and a clinical decompression — don't wait for a chest X-ray in a patient who is actively decompensating.

Always follow decompression with a formal chest tube; neither needle decompression nor finger thoracostomy alone is definitive management.

procedures.description: Subxiphoid needle decompression of tamponade.

blocks.html:
• Pericardial tamponade with hemodynamic compromise (Beck's triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds; or ultrasound-confirmed effusion with tamponade physiology)
  • Peri-arrest or arrest from suspected tamponade, particularly after penetrating chest trauma or in the setting of known pericardial effusion

• None absolute in a hemodynamically unstable patient with confirmed or highly suspected tamponade
  • Traumatic tamponade with an available surgical team and OR access — consider proceeding directly to thoracotomy/sternotomy rather than needle pericardiocentesis, which is often temporizing and less definitive for traumatic hemopericardium

• Long spinal needle (typically 18 ga, 15 cm) or dedicated pericardiocentesis kit
  • Ultrasound with cardiac probe (strongly preferred when time allows)
  • ECG monitoring/lead attached to the needle if using electrocardiographic guidance
  • Syringe, three-way stopcock, guidewire/catheter kit if converting to a pigtail drain

steps.html: Position the patient supine, torso elevated 30-45 degrees if tolerated (brings the effusion closer to the anterior chest wall).
Identify the subxiphoid approach: insert the needle just left and inferior to the xiphoid process, at a 45-degree angle to the skin, aiming toward the left shoulder.
Use ultrasound guidance if available to visualize the needle path directly into the effusion, avoiding the heart, lung, and liver.
Advance slowly while aspirating continuously; a sudden return of non-clotting blood or fluid confirms entry into the pericardial space.
Aspirate as much fluid as needed to restore hemodynamics; even small volumes (50-100 mL) can produce significant improvement in tamponade physiology.
Consider leaving a pigtail catheter in place over a guidewire (Seldinger technique) if reaccumulation is anticipated before definitive surgical management.
Reassess hemodynamics continuously; this is often temporizing — arrange definitive management (surgical drainage, thoracotomy) promptly.

blocks.title: Small volumes can produce large hemodynamic improvement
blocks.html: Don't chase complete drainage at the expense of safety — ultrasound guidance dramatically improves success and safety over blind landmark technique whenever the equipment and time allow.

• Cardiac chamber puncture/laceration, particularly the right ventricle
  • Coronary artery injury
  • Pneumothorax from inadvertent lung puncture
  • Arrhythmia from myocardial irritation — ECG-guided technique can help detect needle-myocardium contact (ST changes/ectopy) before injury occurs
  • Incomplete drainage or reaccumulation if not converted to a pigtail catheter

Ultrasound guidance dramatically improves safety and success compared to blind landmark technique — use it whenever the equipment and time allow.

Small aspirated volumes can produce large hemodynamic improvement in tamponade — don't chase complete drainage at the expense of safety.

In traumatic tamponade with surgical resources available, needle pericardiocentesis is often a bridge, not the definitive answer — keep the surgical team engaged in parallel.

procedures.title: Resuscitative Thoracotomy (Clamshell)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: The last-resort maneuver for the peri-arrest or arrested trauma patient — direct access to the heart, the hilum, and the descending aorta.
procedures.description: Last-resort direct cardiac and hilar access.

blocks.html:
• Penetrating trauma with witnessed loss of vital signs and <15 minutes of prehospital CPR (best outcomes)
  • Penetrating trauma with signs of life on arrival that are lost during resuscitation
  • Blunt trauma with witnessed arrest and <10 minutes of CPR (much lower survival, but still a candidate population at select centers)
  • Suspected pericardial tamponade, massive hemothorax, or air embolism amenable to thoracotomy-based intervention in the peri-arrest patient

• Blunt trauma arrest with prolonged downtime and no signs of life — survival is exceedingly rare and most protocols exclude this group
  • Penetrating trauma with prolonged (>15 min) CPR and no signs of life
  • Injuries clearly incompatible with survival regardless of intervention

• Scalpel (#10 blade), Mayo scissors, rib spreaders (Finochietto retractor)
  • Internal defibrillator paddles
  • Vascular clamps (for aortic cross-clamping)
  • Suction, large-bore IV/central access already in progress
  • Available OR/surgical backup for definitive repair

steps.html: Confirm indication criteria rapidly — mechanism, downtime, and signs of life determine candidacy; this decision must be made in seconds, not minutes.
Make a left anterolateral thoracotomy incision at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, from the sternal border to the posterior axillary line.
Extend to a clamshell (bilateral anterolateral thoracotomy with transverse sternotomy) if right-sided or bilateral pathology is suspected, or if left-sided exposure alone is inadequate.
Insert a rib spreader and open the chest widely.
Open the pericardium longitudinally, anterior to the phrenic nerve, to relieve tamponade if present and expose the heart.
Control cardiac hemorrhage with digital pressure, staples, or sutures as indicated; identify and control any great vessel injury.
Perform internal cardiac massage if in arrest.
Cross-clamp the descending thoracic aorta if hemorrhage control below the diaphragm and improved cerebral/coronary perfusion is the goal.
Defibrillate internally if indicated using internal paddles.
Transition immediately to definitive OR management once any restoration of perfusion is achieved — this procedure is a bridge to definitive repair, not the endpoint.

blocks.title: Indication criteria determine survival more than technique does
blocks.html: Applying this outside validated criteria (mechanism, downtime, signs of life) consumes resources without a realistic survival benefit — know your institution's specific criteria before the patient arrives, not while cutting.

• Extremely high mortality even with correct indication and technique — set expectations with the team accordingly
  • Iatrogenic injury to the heart, great vessels, lung, or phrenic nerve during rapid exposure
  • Failure to control the actual source of hemorrhage/tamponade despite adequate exposure
  • Provider injury (sharp instruments, exposed bone edges) in a high-adrenaline, high-speed procedure — maintain situational awareness for the team's safety too

Indication criteria matter enormously for outcome — this is not a universal salvage maneuver, and applying it outside validated criteria consumes resources without a realistic survival benefit.

Speed of exposure is everything; the incision-to-pericardium interval is the single biggest modifiable time factor.

Know your institution's criteria and have the conversation about candidacy before the patient arrives, not while cutting.

procedures.title: Synchronized Cardioversion vs. Defibrillation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Knowing which button to press, and why the timing of the shock relative to the QRS is the entire distinction between the two.
procedures.description: Timing the shock relative to the QRS — and why it matters.

blocks.html:
Synchronized cardioversion

  • Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a discernible, organized QRS complex: unstable SVT, unstable atrial fibrillation/flutter with rapid ventricular response, unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse

Defibrillation (unsynchronized)

  • Pulseless ventricular fibrillation
  • Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
  • Polymorphic VT (unsynchronized due to the irregular, unpredictable QRS morphology precluding reliable synchronization)

• Stable tachyarrhythmia (no hemodynamic compromise) — pursue pharmacologic management first
  • Synchronized cardioversion should not be attempted on a rhythm without a clear, consistently identifiable QRS for the machine to sync to (e.g., polymorphic VT) — default to unsynchronized defibrillation instead

• Defibrillator/cardioversion-capable monitor with pads or paddles
  • Sedation/analgesia for a conscious, unstable patient prior to synchronized cardioversion when time allows
Synchronized cardioversion

steps.html: Confirm the patient is unstable and the rhythm has a discernible, organized QRS complex.
Attach pads/leads, ensure clear ECG tracing on the monitor.
Activate the synchronization mode on the defibrillator — confirm the sync markers are correctly aligned on each QRS complex before shocking.
Sedate if time and hemodynamic status allow.
Select the appropriate energy level per rhythm (lower initial energies for SVT/atrial arrhythmias, higher for monomorphic VT, per your device and current ACLS guidance).
Deliver the shock — note that with synchronization active, there may be a brief delay between pressing the shock button and actual delivery as the machine times the discharge to the QRS.
Reassess rhythm and pulse immediately after the shock; re-sync and repeat if the arrhythmia persists and the patient remains unstable.

blocks.html: Defibrillation (unsynchronized)

steps.html: Confirm pulseless VF or VT (or polymorphic VT with instability).
Attach pads, ensure no synchronization mode is active.
Select maximum or protocol-appropriate energy per your device.
Announce clear, ensure no one is in contact with the patient or bed.
Deliver the shock immediately without delay.
Resume CPR immediately after the shock without pausing to check rhythm/pulse; reassess at the next scheduled rhythm check per the resuscitation algorithm.

blocks.title: Confirm sync mode every single time before shocking
blocks.html: Many devices default back to unsynchronized mode after each delivery — an unsynchronized shock landing on the T wave of a patient who still has a pulse is the exact mechanism sync mode exists to prevent.

• Delivering an unsynchronized shock on a rhythm with a pulse can precipitate VF if it lands on the T wave (R-on-T phenomenon) — this is the entire reason synchronization exists for stable-QRS tachyarrhythmias
  • Failure to switch out of sync mode when transitioning to a pulseless rhythm can cause the machine to fail to deliver a shock when needed emergently
  • Skin burns or discomfort, particularly with repeated shocks
  • Inadequate sedation for a conscious, unstable patient undergoing synchronized cardioversion

The core distinction is simple once internalized: sync mode times the shock to avoid the vulnerable period of the T wave in a patient who still has a pulse; defibrillation doesn't need to, because there's no organized rhythm or pulse to protect.

After every synchronized cardioversion attempt, re-confirm sync mode is still active before the next shock — many devices default back to unsynchronized mode after each delivery.

If a patient in front of you goes pulseless after a rhythm you were about to synchronize-cardiovert, that's your cue to immediately switch to standard defibrillation and CPR, not to keep pursuing the sync approach.

procedures.title: Targeted Temperature Management Initiation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Post-ROSC neuroprotection — starting the cooling/normothermia protocol in the critical early window after return of spontaneous circulation.
procedures.description: Post-ROSC neuroprotection protocol.

blocks.html:
• Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after cardiac arrest with persistent coma/lack of purposeful response to verbal commands
  • Applies to both shockable and non-shockable initial rhythms per current post-arrest care guidelines

• Patient following commands/purposeful movement after ROSC (TTM is not indicated in a patient who is neurologically intact or rapidly recovering)
  • Active, uncontrolled major hemorrhage where induced hypothermia's coagulopathic effects would be dangerous (relative, favoring strict normothermia target over deeper cooling)
  • Pre-existing terminal condition where the goals of care do not support aggressive post-arrest intervention

• Temperature management device (surface cooling pads/wraps or intravascular cooling catheter system)
  • Continuous core temperature monitoring (esophageal, bladder, or rectal probe)
  • Sedation and, if needed, neuromuscular blockade to prevent shivering
  • Continuous cardiac and hemodynamic monitoring

steps.html: Confirm the indication: comatose, non-purposeful patient after ROSC.
Place continuous core temperature monitoring immediately.

Initiate the cooling device per your institutional target — current guidelines support a target range generally between 32-36°C, with an increasing emphasis on strict normothermia (around 36-37.5°C) with fever avoidance as an accepted alternative strategy at many centers; follow your institution's specific protocol.
Sedate adequately and add neuromuscular blockade if shivering occurs and is not controlled by sedation alone — shivering generates heat and undermines the target temperature.
Maintain the target temperature for the protocol-defined duration (commonly 24 hours at target, per most published protocols).
Rewarm slowly and in a controlled fashion per protocol (typically no faster than 0.25-0.5°C per hour) to avoid rebound hyperthermia, electrolyte shifts, and hemodynamic instability.
Maintain strict normothermia and fever avoidance for an extended period after the active cooling/rewarming phase, as post-arrest fever is independently associated with worse neurologic outcomes.

blocks.title: Fever avoidance is the one point of broad consensus
blocks.html: Whatever specific temperature target the institution uses, post-arrest fever is independently associated with worse neurologic outcomes — treat shivering aggressively and early since it both signals and obstructs reaching target.

• Shivering, which increases metabolic demand and can undermine target temperature achievement — treat proactively with sedation/paralysis rather than reactively
  • Electrolyte shifts (hypokalemia during cooling, rebound hyperkalemia during rewarming)
  • Coagulopathy and increased bleeding risk at deeper hypothermia targets
  • Arrhythmia risk, particularly bradycardia, at lower temperature targets
  • Rebound hyperthermia if rewarming is too rapid or fever isn't proactively managed afterward

The single most important actionable step is avoiding fever, whatever specific temperature target your institution uses — this is the one point of broad consensus across the evolving TTM literature.

Start temperature management as early as possible after ROSC is confirmed; delayed initiation is associated with reduced benefit.

Treat shivering aggressively and early — it is both a sign the target isn't being met and an active obstacle to reaching it.

procedures.title: Transcutaneous & Transvenous Pacing
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: From pads on the chest to a wire in the right ventricle — bridging unstable bradycardia to a definitive rhythm.
procedures.description: Bridging unstable bradycardia to a definitive rhythm.

blocks.html:
• Symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine and/or refractory to initial pharmacologic management
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, third-degree) with hemodynamic instability
  • Bradycardic peri-arrest rhythms where pacing is part of the resuscitation algorithm
  • Transvenous pacing specifically indicated when transcutaneous pacing fails to capture, is not tolerated, or a more durable/reliable pacing solution is needed pending definitive management

• Severe hypothermia with bradycardia (pacing is generally ineffective and not recommended until rewarming, per most protocols — the heart is often refractory to pacing at low core temperatures)
  • Transvenous pacing: coagulopathy or inability to obtain safe central venous access (relative, weighed against the urgency of the indication)

Transcutaneous pacing

  • Cardiac monitor/defibrillator with pacing capability
  • Pacing pads (anterior-posterior placement preferred)
  • Sedation/analgesia for a conscious patient — transcutaneous pacing is uncomfortable

Transvenous pacing

  • Central venous access kit (internal jugular or subclavian preferred for lead stability)
  • Transvenous pacing wire/catheter
  • External pacing generator
  • Fluoroscopy or ECG-guided placement confirmation if available
Transcutaneous pacing

steps.html: Apply pacing pads in the anterior-posterior position for optimal capture.
Set the pacer to demand mode (synchronized to the patient's intrinsic rhythm) unless asystole, in which case use fixed/asynchronous mode.
Set the initial rate (typically 60-80 bpm as a starting target).
Increase output (mA) gradually from a low starting point until electrical capture is confirmed — a paced QRS complex following each pacing spike, correlating with a palpable pulse.
Set the final output slightly above the capture threshold for a safety margin.
Provide sedation/analgesia promptly, as transcutaneous pacing causes significant discomfort in an awake patient.
Confirm mechanical capture (palpable pulse corresponding to the paced rate), not just electrical capture on the monitor.

blocks.html: Transvenous pacing

steps.html: Obtain central venous access, typically right internal jugular or left subclavian for the most direct path to the right ventricle.
Advance the pacing wire through the introducer sheath toward the right ventricle, using ECG guidance (injury pattern on the pacing wire's intracardiac ECG) or fluoroscopy if available.
Connect the wire to the external pacing generator once positioned.
Set output and sensitivity, confirm capture (paced rhythm on the monitor with correlating pulse).
Secure the wire and generator, obtain a confirmatory chest radiograph for lead position.

blocks.title: Electrical capture is not mechanical capture
blocks.html: Always confirm a palpable pulse correlating with the paced rhythm before considering the patient stabilized — pacing spikes on the monitor without a pulse behind them is still pulseless electrical activity.

• Failure to capture — reassess pad placement/wire position and increase output as needed
  • Electrical capture without mechanical capture (pulseless electrical activity despite pacing spikes) — always confirm a palpable pulse, not just the monitor tracing
  • Significant discomfort with transcutaneous pacing if sedation is inadequate
  • Lead perforation, arrhythmia, or cardiac tamponade with transvenous wire placement
  • Lead dislodgement with patient movement if not adequately secured

Electrical capture on the monitor is not the same as effective pacing — always confirm a palpable pulse correlating with the paced rhythm before considering the patient stabilized.

Transcutaneous pacing is a bridge while transvenous access is arranged in most non-transient cases — don't treat it as a definitive solution if the bradycardia is expected to persist.

Sedate early for transcutaneous pacing in an awake patient; this is one of the more uncomfortable interventions in the resuscitation toolkit.

procedures.title: Manual Uterine Massage & Bimanual Compression
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Obstetric
procedures.subtitle: First-line mechanical management of uterine atony — the hands-on step that often works before any medication does.
procedures.description: First-line mechanical management of uterine atony.

blocks.html:
• Postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony (a boggy, poorly contracted uterus on palpation, with ongoing vaginal bleeding after delivery)
  • First-line intervention alongside uterotonic medication administration

• None absolute in postpartum hemorrhage from suspected atony
  • Hemorrhage from a source other than atony (laceration, retained products, coagulopathy) will not respond to massage/compression alone — reassess promptly if bleeding continues despite a firm, well-contracted uterus

• Gloved hands — this is a manual technique requiring no specialized equipment
  • Uterotonic medications on hand as concurrent pharmacologic management (oxytocin first-line, with additional agents per protocol for refractory atony)
Fundal massage

steps.html: Place one hand on the abdomen at the level of the uterine fundus.
Massage firmly in a circular or kneading motion to stimulate uterine contraction.
Reassess uterine tone frequently — a well-contracted uterus should feel firm, like a clenched fist, rather than soft/boggy.

blocks.html: Bimanual compression

steps.html: Insert one hand into the vagina, forming a fist, and place it in the anterior fornix, pushing against the anterior surface of the uterus.
Place the other hand on the abdomen behind the uterine fundus.
Compress the uterus firmly between both hands, applying sustained pressure.
Continue compression while uterotonic medications take effect and while arranging for any additional interventions (balloon tamponade, surgical management) if bleeding is refractory.
Maintain compression until bleeding is controlled and uterine tone is restored, or until more definitive management is ready to proceed.

blocks.title: Start it the moment atony is suspected, not after medications are running
blocks.html: This is a first-line, no-equipment-needed intervention that belongs in parallel with calling for uterotonics, not sequentially after them.

• Continued hemorrhage despite adequate technique — reassess for an alternate cause (laceration, retained products, coagulopathy) rather than persisting indefinitely with massage alone
  • Provider fatigue during prolonged bimanual compression — this can be physically demanding to sustain and may require provider rotation
  • Delayed escalation to definitive management (balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolization, surgical intervention) if massage/compression is relied upon past the point of effectiveness

This is a first-line, immediate, no-equipment-needed intervention — start it the moment atony is suspected, in parallel with calling for uterotonic medications, not sequentially.

A uterus that firms up under your hand and then goes soft again the moment you stop massaging is telling you atony is ongoing and you need to escalate pharmacologic/procedural management, not just keep massaging indefinitely.

Don't let bimanual compression become a substitute for identifying a non-atony cause of hemorrhage if the uterus is actually firm and bleeding continues.

procedures.title: Perimortem Cesarean Section / Resuscitative Hysterotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Obstetric
procedures.subtitle: The 4-minute rule: a maternal resuscitation maneuver first, a delivery second. Speed and aortocaval decompression over sterility and anatomic precision.
procedures.description: The 4-minute rule — maternal resuscitation first.

blocks.html:
• Maternal cardiac arrest at or beyond ~20 weeks gestational age (fundus at or above the umbilicus), with no ROSC after initial resuscitative measures
  • Goal is dual: relieve aortocaval compression to improve maternal resuscitation, and deliver a potentially viable fetus
  • A maternal resuscitation procedure first — it improves maternal cardiac output even if fetal viability is uncertain or fetal demise has already occurred

• True contraindications are minimal given the life-threatening nature of the indication
  • Gestational age clearly and reliably below viability/umbilical fundal height (relative — aortocaval relief may still benefit the mother even below classic viability thresholds)
  • Do not delay for imaging, fetal heart tones, or transport to an OR — this is a bedside/field procedure when indicated

• Scalpel (#10 blade) — the only truly essential instrument
  • Whatever is immediately available: hemostats, scissors, retractors, suction if present
  • Should not require a dedicated tray — delay to gather equipment defeats the purpose

steps.html: Continue high-quality maternal CPR throughout — compressions and airway management do not stop for this procedure.
Trigger the decision at the 4-minute mark of maternal arrest without ROSC (target incision at 4 minutes, delivery by 5 minutes — the “4-minute rule”).
No time for antiseptic prep, anesthesia, or patient positioning changes — proceed immediately at the bedside/scene.
Make a vertical midline incision from the umbilicus to the pubic symphysis through skin, subcutaneous tissue, and fascia.
Enter the peritoneum bluntly.
Identify the uterus; make a vertical (classical) incision through the lower uterine segment/uterine wall — faster and more forgiving of imprecise anatomy under crisis conditions.
Extend the uterine incision with fingers (not scalpel) once the uterine cavity is entered, to avoid fetal injury.
Deliver the fetus, clamp and cut the cord, hand off immediately to a neonatal resuscitation team/pathway.
Deliver the placenta if readily accomplished, but do not delay ongoing maternal resuscitation for this.
Continue maternal CPR and resuscitation — aortocaval decompression from evacuating the uterus often improves venous return and compression effectiveness immediately.
Pack the open abdomen/uterus if maternal ROSC is achieved and hemorrhage control is needed en route to definitive surgical management.

blocks.title: This is a maternal resuscitation maneuver, not a delivery decision
blocks.html: Framing it that way to the team — "we are decompressing the aorta and vena cava" — reduces the hesitation that is the single biggest reason the 4-minute window is missed in real events.

• Delay is the dominant failure mode — teams hesitate waiting for confirmation, equipment, or a “better” location; effectiveness drops rapidly after minute 5
  • Fetal laceration from scalpel extension of the uterine incision — extend with fingers once inside the uterine cavity
  • Underestimating gestational age at the bedside — fundal height at or above umbilicus is the trigger, not a documented gestational age
  • Stopping compressions during the procedure — compressions continue throughout
  • Failure to have a neonatal resuscitation plan ready — a second team/provider should be staged for the newborn before incision if any warning exists

This is fundamentally a maternal resuscitation maneuver — frame it that way to the team to reduce hesitation. “We are decompressing the aorta and vena cava” gets action faster than “we are delivering a baby.”

Speed over sterility, speed over anatomic precision — the 4-to-5-minute window is the entire clinical rationale.

Vertical skin and uterine incisions are faster and more forgiving than transverse under crisis conditions; save the cosmetic technique for controlled OR deliveries.

Announce the time of arrest loudly and repeatedly so the 4-minute trigger isn't missed in the chaos of a resuscitation.

procedures.title: Symphysiotomy & Procedural Shoulder Dystocia Maneuvers
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Obstetric
procedures.subtitle: The escalation ladder for shoulder dystocia, ending in a rarely-needed but field-relevant last resort.
procedures.description: The escalation ladder, ending in a rare last resort.

blocks.html:
• Shoulder dystocia: failure of the fetal shoulders to deliver spontaneously after delivery of the head, often recognized by the "turtle sign" (head retracting against the perineum)
  • Symphysiotomy specifically reserved for shoulder dystocia refractory to standard maneuvers, in settings without immediate access to cesarean delivery

• Symphysiotomy: any setting with timely access to cesarean delivery should default to that option instead — this is a resource-limited/field last resort, not a routine escalation step
  • Standard maneuvers have essentially no contraindications in true shoulder dystocia given the acute fetal risk

• None required for positional/manual maneuvers
  • Scalpel, local anesthetic if performing symphysiotomy
Escalation sequence for shoulder dystocia

steps.html: Call for help immediately and note the time — shoulder dystocia is a time-critical fetal emergency.
McRoberts maneuver: sharply flex the mother's hips against her abdomen, flattening the sacrum and rotating the pubic symphysis, often resolving the dystocia alone.
Apply suprapubic pressure simultaneously (not fundal pressure, which worsens impaction) directed downward and laterally to adduct the anterior shoulder.
If unresolved, proceed to internal maneuvers: deliver the posterior arm, or rotational maneuvers (Rubin or Woods screw) to rotate the fetal shoulders into an oblique plane.
Consider the Gaskin (all-fours) maneuver if the mother's position allows and other techniques have failed.
As a last resort in an unresolved dystocia with fetal compromise and no timely surgical option, consider deliberate clavicular fracture or, exceedingly rarely, symphysiotomy.

blocks.html: Symphysiotomy (last-resort technique)

steps.html: Confirm all standard maneuvers have failed and cesarean delivery is not accessible in the necessary timeframe.
Infiltrate local anesthetic over the pubic symphysis if time and circumstances allow.
With the mother's legs supported and hips moderately abducted, make an incision through the skin and the fibrocartilaginous symphyseal joint at the midline.
Apply controlled pressure only as needed to create additional pelvic outlet space — this is a measured, not maximal, separation.
Proceed immediately with delivery of the impacted shoulder once adequate space is achieved.
Manage the symphyseal disruption post-delivery per orthopedic/surgical follow-up — this creates a significant maternal injury that requires definitive management afterward.

blocks.title: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves most cases
blocks.html: Never apply fundal pressure — it worsens impaction rather than relieving it. Symphysiotomy is a genuine last resort reserved for settings without timely cesarean access, not a routine escalation step.

• Brachial plexus injury or clavicular/humeral fracture to the fetus from excessive traction during any maneuver — avoid fundal pressure and excessive axial traction throughout
  • Maternal perineal/vaginal trauma from internal maneuvers
  • Symphysiotomy: significant maternal pelvic instability, pain, and long-term morbidity — this is a genuinely last-resort technique with substantial maternal cost
  • Delayed escalation through the maneuver sequence in a truly refractory dystocia, worsening fetal hypoxic risk

McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves the large majority of shoulder dystocias — most cases never need to progress further down this list.

Never apply fundal pressure in shoulder dystocia — it worsens impaction rather than relieving it; suprapubic pressure is the correct external maneuver.

Symphysiotomy belongs in the field/resource-limited-setting category of this library specifically because it is almost never the right choice when a timely cesarean is available — know your setting's actual escalation pathway before assuming this technique applies.

procedures.title: Active Internal Rewarming (ECMO/CPB Crossover)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Environmental
procedures.subtitle: Core rewarming for severe hypothermia with cardiac instability — where extracorporeal circulation becomes both the rewarming method and the resuscitation.
procedures.description: Core rewarming for hypothermic cardiac instability.

blocks.html:
• Severe hypothermia (core temperature typically <28°C) with cardiac instability, arrhythmia (including ventricular fibrillation), or cardiac arrest
  • Hypothermic cardiac arrest, where standard resuscitation and defibrillation are often ineffective until adequate rewarming is achieved — extracorporeal rewarming is the definitive management in this population

• None absolute in hypothermic cardiac arrest with a survivable overall clinical picture (the guiding principle: "nobody is dead until warm and dead")
  • Injuries or comorbidities incompatible with survival regardless of rewarming (as with any ECMO candidacy decision)

• ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) circuit and cannulation equipment (see ECMO Cannulation entry)
  • Continuous core temperature monitoring
  • Full resuscitation equipment, as CPR and standard ACLS measures continue in parallel during cannulation

steps.html: Continue high-quality CPR and standard resuscitation measures throughout — do not withhold compressions while awaiting rewarming capability.

Recognize that standard defibrillation and many ACLS medications are often ineffective below a core temperature threshold (commonly cited around 30°C) — limit repeated defibrillation attempts and medication administration per hypothermia-specific arrest protocols until adequate rewarming is underway.

Activate ECMO/CPB team and cannulate per the standard ECMO cannulation framework (see the ECMO Cannulation Prep & Activation entry), using this specifically as both circulatory support and a rewarming method.
Once on circuit, rewarm gradually and per protocol — controlled rewarming rate, avoiding the afterdrop and rewarming shock associated with overly rapid temperature correction.
Continue resuscitation efforts as core temperature rises, reattempting defibrillation and standard ACLS interventions once temperature thresholds are crossed per protocol.
Monitor closely for reperfusion/rewarming complications: arrhythmia, electrolyte shifts, and hemodynamic instability as peripheral vasodilation occurs with rewarming.

blocks.title: Nobody is dead until warm and dead
blocks.html: Profound hypothermia is neuroprotective, and standard defibrillation/ACLS medications are often ineffective below roughly 30°C — don't burn through hypothermia-specific attempt limits before rewarming capability is underway.

• Afterdrop (continued core temperature decline immediately after rewarming initiation) from cold peripheral blood returning centrally
  • Rewarming shock from peripheral vasodilation outpacing volume status
  • Arrhythmia during the rewarming process, particularly as temperature crosses certain thresholds
  • Delayed recognition that standard resuscitation measures are unlikely to succeed without rewarming capability, delaying ECMO/CPB activation

"Nobody is dead until warm and dead" is the governing principle — profound hypothermia is neuroprotective, and patients have survived prolonged arrest with intact neurologic outcomes after extracorporeal rewarming.

This is functionally the same activation and cannulation process as standard ECPR (see the ECMO Cannulation Prep & Activation entry), applied specifically to the hypothermic arrest population where the circuit does double duty as both circulatory support and the rewarming method itself.

Don't burn through your hypothermia-specific ACLS medication/defibrillation allowances early — most hypothermia protocols cap attempts below a temperature threshold precisely because they're unlikely to work until the myocardium is warm enough to respond.

procedures.title: Escharotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Environmental
procedures.subtitle: Releasing the constricting, unyielding burn eschar before it compromises circulation or ventilation.
procedures.description: Releasing constricting burn eschar from limb or chest.

blocks.html:
• Circumferential full-thickness (or near full-thickness) burns to an extremity with signs of vascular compromise (diminished/absent distal pulses, capillary refill delay, paresthesia, worsening pain)
  • Circumferential torso/chest burns causing restrictive impairment of ventilation (reduced chest wall compliance, rising peak airway pressures in a ventilated patient)

• None absolute in the presence of true vascular or ventilatory compromise from constricting eschar
  • Partial-thickness burns without circumferential involvement or compromise (escharotomy is not indicated in the absence of compartment-type physiology)

• Scalpel or electrocautery
  • Hemostatic agents/dressings for the resulting wound
Extremity escharotomy

steps.html: Identify the affected extremity with signs of vascular compromise distal to the circumferential burn.

Mark the incision lines along the mid-medial and/or mid-lateral aspects of the limb, avoiding major neurovascular structures (e.g., staying anterior/posterior to the medial epicondyle at the elbow, avoiding the peroneal nerve at the fibular head).

Incise through the full thickness of the eschar (this tissue is insensate in full-thickness burns, so anesthesia is often unnecessary directly over the eschar, though surrounding viable tissue may require analgesia) down to but not through the underlying fascia/subcutaneous fat.
Extend the incision the full length of the circumferential burn, across joints if the burn crosses them.
Confirm the release — the wound edges should visibly separate/gape, and distal perfusion (pulses, capillary refill) should improve.
Achieve hemostasis of the incised edges as needed and dress the wound.

blocks.html: Chest/torso escharotomy

steps.html: Identify circumferential chest/torso burns with restrictive ventilatory compromise.
Mark incision lines along the anterior axillary lines bilaterally, connected by a transverse incision along the costal margin if needed to fully release the chest wall.
Incise through the full thickness of the eschar along the marked lines.
Reassess ventilatory mechanics (chest wall compliance, peak pressures if ventilated) after release.

blocks.title: Reassess immediately after the incision to confirm it worked
blocks.html: An inadequate-length incision that doesn't extend across the full circumferential burn (or across an involved joint) is the most common reason for persistent vascular or ventilatory compromise after escharotomy.

• Bleeding from the incision, particularly if extended too deep into viable, vascularized tissue rather than staying within the eschar
  • Incomplete release if the incision doesn't extend the full length of the circumferential burn or across an involved joint
  • Injury to underlying neurovascular structures if incision lines are not planned correctly for the specific anatomic location
  • Missed compartment syndrome distinct from the eschar itself — escharotomy releases the burned skin's constriction; a true muscle compartment syndrome underneath may still require separate fasciotomy

This procedure targets the eschar specifically, not the deeper fascia — don't confuse it with fasciotomy, which is a separate, deeper procedure for true compartment syndrome.

Reassess distal perfusion or ventilatory mechanics immediately after the incision to confirm the release actually worked — an inadequate-length incision is a common reason for persistent compromise.

The eschar itself is typically insensate in full-thickness injury, which is part of why this procedure can often be performed with minimal local anesthesia directly over the burned tissue.

procedures.title: Field Amputation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Mass Casualty
procedures.subtitle: An exceedingly rare, last-resort extrication technique — entrapment with an unsalvageable limb and a threat to life that transport delay would worsen.
procedures.description: Rare last-resort extrication technique.

blocks.html:
• Entrapment of a limb that cannot be extricated by any other means, where the limb is already unsalvageable (mangled, non-viable) and continued entrapment poses an immediate threat to the patient's life
  • Confined-space or structural collapse scenarios where standard extrication (cutting the entrapping structure rather than the patient) has been exhausted and is not feasible within a survivable timeframe

• Any scenario where standard extrication techniques (cutting away the entrapping material rather than the patient) remain feasible, even if slower — this is always the preferred approach
  • A potentially salvageable limb where extrication delay does not pose an immediate life threat

• Amputation kit if available (surgical saw or heavy shears, hemostatic/tourniquet equipment, sedation/analgesia)
  • Whatever cutting instrument is available in a true improvised scenario
  • Tourniquet(s) for immediate hemorrhage control

steps.html: Exhaust all standard extrication options first — this procedure is a genuine last resort, typically performed by a physician or surgeon responding to the scene in coordination with technical rescue/fire services, not a routine field decision.

Confirm the limb is non-viable and that continued entrapment is an immediate threat to survival (structural collapse progression, fire, rising water, or physiologic deterioration from prolonged crush injury).
Provide maximal available analgesia/sedation given the circumstances.
Apply a proximal tourniquet before amputation to control hemorrhage from the outset.
Amputate through the most distal viable/accessible point that achieves extrication, using whatever surgical or improvised means are available.
Complete extrication and immediately transition to standard trauma/hemorrhage resuscitation, including reassessment of tourniquet effectiveness and definitive surgical management planning.

blocks.title: Every standard extrication option comes first
blocks.html: This is one of the rarest procedures in the entire library for a reason — nearly every entrapment scenario resolves through cutting the environment, not the patient. Tourniquet control must be established before the cut, not improvised after.

• Massive hemorrhage if tourniquet control is not established before or immediately upon amputation
  • Profound psychological impact on both patient and providers — this is one of the most extreme interventions in emergency medicine and should be recognized as such for the entire team
  • Infection risk given the non-sterile, improvised nature of most field amputation scenarios
  • Crush syndrome/reperfusion physiology if a tourniquet is released or extrication occurs after prolonged entrapment without appropriate resuscitation first (see Crush Syndrome/Entrapment content elsewhere in Crisis Management)

This is one of the rarest procedures in the entire library for a reason — nearly every entrapment scenario resolves through cutting the environment, not the patient. Treat this as the true last resort it is.

Tourniquet control before the cut, not after — hemorrhage control needs to be established as part of the plan, not improvised in the moment of extrication.

This procedure is typically physician/surgeon-led when performed in the field (e.g., HEMS physician response, USAR medical team) rather than a standard paramedic-level intervention — know your scope and your system's activation pathway for this exact scenario before you ever need it.

procedures.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen Coordination & Prep
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Environmental
procedures.subtitle: Decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism — 100% oxygen first, chamber logistics in parallel, altitude avoided at every step of transport.
procedures.description: DCS/AGE — 100% oxygen first, altitude avoided.

blocks.html:
• Decompression sickness (Type I — pain/limb, or Type II — neurologic, cardiopulmonary, cutis marmorata)
  • Arterial gas embolism from diving, iatrogenic sources (surgery, central line, hemodialysis), or barotrauma
  • Severe carbon monoxide poisoning with neurologic findings or loss of consciousness (frequent co-management pathway with the same chambers/teams)
  • Any diver with new neurologic, pulmonary, or cardiovascular symptoms after a dive, regardless of dive profile — err toward treatment when suspicion exists

• Untreated pneumothorax — absolute contraindication until a chest tube is placed (pressure changes in the chamber can convert to tension physiology)
  • Relative: certain chemotherapy agents, uncontrolled seizure disorder, severe COPD with bullae, claustrophobia (multiplace chambers can accommodate with support)
  • None of these should delay initial stabilization and 100% oxygen while transport/chamber access is arranged

• High-flow 100% oxygen delivery (non-rebreather or demand valve) for immediate use before and during transport
  • IV access and isotonic fluids (dehydration worsens bubble formation/tissue injury)
  • Monitoring: continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor
  • Communication line to nearest hyperbaric chamber (know your regional chamber contact before you need it — DAN emergency line 919-684-9111 for diving-specific consultation)
  • Transport plan that avoids further altitude exposure (ground transport preferred; if air transport unavoidable, lowest safe cabin altitude, ideally pressurized to sea level)

steps.html: Place patient supine or left lateral for AGE (historical Trendelenburg positioning is no longer recommended — it can worsen cerebral edema).
Start 100% oxygen immediately via non-rebreather or demand valve, regardless of transport time — the single highest-yield intervention before chamber arrival.
Establish IV access; begin isotonic fluid resuscitation to address hemoconcentration.
Perform a focused neurologic exam and document it — serial exams matter for tracking response and guiding chamber protocol.
Rule out or address pneumothorax before any chamber transport — this is a hard gate.
Contact the nearest operational hyperbaric chamber directly — describe presentation, dive/exposure history, and confirm chamber availability and readiness.
Arrange transport that avoids altitude gain; if fixed-wing transport is required, coordinate cabin pressurization to sea level or the lowest achievable altitude.
Continue 100% oxygen and monitoring throughout transport.
On arrival, hand off directly to hyperbaric medicine team with full history: dive profile (depth/time), symptom onset timing, treatments given en route.
Anticipate treatment via a US Navy Treatment Table (e.g., Table 6) or institutional equivalent — this decision belongs to the hyperbaric team.

blocks.title: Oxygen first, logistics in parallel
blocks.html: 100% oxygen is free and immediate — start it before chamber transport is even confirmed, and never let arranging transport delay the one intervention that's already available at the bedside.

• Delaying oxygen while arranging chamber logistics — start O2 first, coordinate transport in parallel, not sequentially
  • Missing a pneumothorax before pressurization — converts a treatable emergency into a chamber-induced tension physiology crisis
  • Air transport at altitude without addressing cabin pressurization, which worsens bubble expansion (Boyle's law)
  • Underestimating symptom severity in early/mild presentations that later progress — low threshold to treat empirically
  • Losing time locating a chamber — this should be a pre-identified resource, not a search performed during the emergency

100% oxygen is free, immediate, and works — start it before you've even confirmed chamber transport, and never stop it while awaiting or during transport.

Have your regional chamber's contact number and DAN's line saved before you ever need them.

Ground transport beats air transport unless the ground time is prohibitively long — altitude is the enemy in both DCS and AGE.

This is a “call early, treat now” pathway — engage hyperbaric medicine as soon as suspicion is reasonable.
